newsitem.title: INDONESIA: GM urged to continue Indonesian investment.
newsitem.headline: GM urged to continue Indonesian investment.

text.p: U.S. carmaker General Motors should ignore Indonesia's car policy which offered privileges to only one manufacturer and should expand investment in a potentially huge market, GM's local partner said on Thursday.

Probosutedjo, president commissioner of General Motors Buana Indonesia (GMBI), told reporters he had urged GM to expand its operations here because of the market potential of a nation home to nearly 200 million people.

"I have already told General Motors in Detroit not to be hesitant to invest in Indonesia as the future market here will be huge," Probosutedjo, half-brother of President Suharto, told a news conference.

"The Indonesian market in the future will be much bigger than Thailand," Probosutedjo said at a ceremony marking the third anniversary of the founding of GMBI, a joint-venture with GM in which he owns 40 percent through PT Garmak.

In February, PT Timor Putra Nasional, a joint venture between Suharto's youngest son Hutomo Mandala Putra and Kia Motors of South Korea, was given special tax and tariff breaks to produce the Timor sedan as a national car if it met local content targets.
The Timor must meet a 20 percent local content target after the first year and 60 percent by the third year to be fully exempt from import duties and luxury tax.
Japan, the United States and the European Union said the policy violated regulations of the World Trade Organisation.
A number of foreign car makers, including GM, said they had deferred further investment in Indonesia until the impact of the car policy was clear.
GM said it had invested $110 million in its Indonesian assembly plant. It recently announced a $750 million car project in Thailand.

William Botwick, GMBI president director, said he did not expect his company to be significantly affected by the entry of the Timor into the market next month because the firm's flagship vehicle, the Opel Blazer, competed in a different market sector.
The four-door 1,600 cc Timor sedan will sell for about 35 million rupiah ($15,000), while the five-door multi-purpose off-road 2,200 cc Blazer retails for 70 million rupiah.
Botwick said on Thursday that GMBI planned to export up to 1,000 units of the Blazer to South Africa, Namibia, Kenya and Malaysia in 1997.

Production of the Blazer, which has 40 percent local content, began in January and the company expects to make around 6,000 units in 1996, as well as assemble 1,000 units of the mostly imported Optima sedan.
Probosutedjo said GMBI hoped to raise the level of local content of the Blazer to 60 percent within one year. But this still did not qualify the company for tax breaks.
